translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki meet often in their local area, they have identical expressions and ways of speaking.
Especially their way of eating sweets was similar, both were breaking off small pieces of the cookie with their manicured hands and bringing it to their mouths.
I wonder if it has always been like this, but when I try to remember, my memory is vague.
I wonder if the small habits and gestures they showed when we met last time have since drifted away somewhere.
Miho is now married, has bought a second-hand detached house in her hometown, and often gathers with friends there.

Although I sometimes feel reluctant because I have to work part-time again tomorrow, it's my only connection with the world outside of the convenience store and a valuable opportunity to interact with other "normal thirty-something women" of my age, so I try as much as possible to respond to Miho's invitations.
Today, the members were Miho, Yukari with her still small child, Satsuki who is married but has no children yet, and me.
We brought cakes to Miho's house and had tea.
At that moment, for the first time, I was able to become a part of the world.
I thought, now, I have been born.
That day, I was truly born as a normal part of the world.
For two weeks before the opening, we formed pairs and practiced earnestly, pretending to serve imaginary customers while being supervised by other employees.

Looking the "customer" in the eye and giving a small nod with a smile, placing sanitary products in a paper bag, separating hot items from cold ones, disinfecting hands with alcohol when asked to handle fast food.

In order to get used to handling money, there was real money in the cash register, but the word "training" was prominently printed on the receipt, and since the person across from me was a part-time colleague wearing the same uniform, it somehow felt like playing make-believe shopping.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was a "normal" child, unlike me.
But that didn't mean she kept her distance; on the contrary, she looked up to me.
When my younger sister was being scolded by our mother for something ordinary, differing from me, I approached our mother and asked, "Why are you angry?"
Whenever my questioning of our mother ended a sermon, presumably because she felt protected by me, my sister always said "thank you.
As I was not very interested in sweets or toys, I often gave them to my younger sister.
Therefore, my younger sister always followed me around.
"Dad, you like yakitori, so let's grill and eat this today.
I repeated it with clear pronunciation, wondering if it had not been heard well.
My mother was taken aback, and the mother of another child next to us must have been surprised too; her eyes, nostrils, and mouth all opened wide at once.
Seeing his strange face made me want to laugh, but watching him stare at my hands, I realized that one wasn't enough.
"Should I get more?"
As she glanced at two or three sparrows walking side by side nearby, my mother who finally came to her senses called out desperately in a scolding tone, "Keiko!"
"Let's make a grave for the little bird and bury it.
See, everyone is crying too.
It's lonely since our friend died, isn't it?
"Poor thing, isn't it?"
"Why? Even though they're already dead.
At my question, my mother was at a loss for words.
I quickly put canned coffee, cigarettes, and a hot dog into a small-sized bag.
In the meantime, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket suddenly reached into his chest pocket as if he'd had an idea.
From that gesture, I instantly judged that he would pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
Nodding lightly, I accept the canned coffee offered by the male customer.
"Ah, and one of number five cigarettes," "Understood.
He swiftly pulled out a pack of Marlboro Light Menthol and scanned it at the register.
"Please touch for age verification.
Seeing the man's gaze shift smoothly to the showcase filled with fast food as he touched the screen, I stopped moving my fingers.
"I could ask 'Would you like anything?, but when the customer seems indecisive about purchasing, I make it a rule to step back and wait.
Reacting to the faint sound of coins clinking, I turned and shifted my gaze towards the cash register.
Many of the people who jingle coins in their pockets or hands are looking to quickly buy cigarettes or a newspaper, so they are sensitive to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there was a man approaching the register with a can of coffee in one hand and his other hand stuffed in his pocket.
Moving swiftly inside the store, I slid into the cash register counter and stood waiting inside so as not to keep the customers waiting.
The convenience store is filled with noise.
The sound of the chime as a customer enters, accompanied by the voice of an idol promoting new products over the store's in-house broadcast.
The sound of scanning barcodes following the shopkeeper's call.
The sound of items being placed into a basket, the rustling of bread bags, and the clicking of heels walking around the store.
Everything blends together, becoming the "sound of a convenience store," continuously touching my eardrums.
